title: AIR: Rethinking Image-Text Offset Alignment in Multimodal Contrastive Representation Space
claim: Assumed alignment between visual and textual offsets breaks down as concept distance grows, so we iteratively refine text offsets to improve results.
layout: 3 panels: analysis top-left, method top-right, qualitative image grid across bottom
description: A three-part composite figure. Panel (a), on a pink background, shows a circular embedding space. Orange dots (image embeddings) and blue triangles (text embeddings) are joined by orange and blue arrows for dog and wolf concepts. Red and green dashed ellipses mark large and small misalignment. Red and green arrows link two points to a scatter plot of offset misalignment against concept distance, which has a rising trend line. Below the plot is a small table comparing Scottish Terrier and Grey Wolf to Bernese Mountain Dog. Panel (b), on a cream background, shows the AIR method in another circle: a text offset is iteratively refined, with dashed blue triangles, and image embeddings step along a path toward the target. A legend sits above the circle. Panel (c) is a wide qualitative grid. Face photos go to sketches across NADA, IPL, SVL, HGAN and AIR, with AIR outlined in green. Motorcycle edits compare Style-Editor with AIR and internet examples.
caption: Our contributions: (a) We question the assumption of image-text offset alignment and perform a comprehensive analysis of offset alignment in multimodal contrastive representation space. Our analysis reveals not only noticeable misalignment between image offsets (orange arrow) and text offsets (blue arrow), but also a meaningful positive correlation between offset misalignment and concept distance. For example, in the ImageNet-1K dataset, the “Grey Wolf” is a more distant concept to the “Bernese Mountain Dog” (concept distance=0.426) than the “Scottish Terrier” (concept distance=0.307). Accordingly, “Grey Wolf” →“Bernese Mountain Dog” has higher offset misalignment than “Scottish Terrier” →“Bernese Mountain Dog” (0.576 vs 0.285). This misalignment is overlooked in existing uses of image-text offsets (Sec. 3). (b) Leveraging our discovery, we propose Adaptation with Iterative Refinement (AIR) to iteratively refine text offsets and mitigate the downstream effect of offset misalignment for text-driven visual transformations, which we refer as guidance misalignment (Sec. 4). (c) Our proposed AIR consistently reduces the guidance misalignment and enables SOTA performance in important text-guided generative modeling tasks, e.g., capturing rich target concepts’ style and details across diverse setups. (see Sec. 5 and Sec. C.3 for detailed results).
abstract: Image-text offset alignment, which refers to the consistency between visual transformation directions and their corresponding textual transformation directions, has become an important relational property in multimodal contrastive representation spaces such as CLIP and SigLIP. This property plays a central role in text-driven visual transformation tasks, including generative model domain adaptation and text-guided object-centric image editing, where textual offsets are used to guide visual transformations. These methods fundamentally rely on the assumption that image and text offsets are well aligned, such that textual transformation directions can provide reliable guidance for corresponding visual transformations. However, the validity of this alignment assumption has not been systematically examined. In this work, we question this foundational assumption by conducting a comprehensive empirical analysis of image-text offset alignment in multimodal contrastive representation space. Our findings reveal not only noticeable offset misalignment but also a meaningful positive correlation between image-text offset misalignment and semantic concept distance across six large datasets and eight contrastive vision-language models. Based on this discovery, we propose Adaptation with Iterative Refinement (AIR), a method that iteratively refines text offsets through anchor sampling and our proposed concept description learning to mitigate the downstream effect of image-text offset misalignment and improve guidance accuracy. Comprehensive experiments on zero-shot generative model domain adaptation and text-guided object-centric image editing across 40 setups, including qualitative, quantitative, and user studies, consistently show that AIR enables state-of-the-art performance in these tasks.
